items: HFT is a subset, not every algo
props.closer: Build systems that can say no.

captions: Daily trading algorithms.
How machines trade, and the India reality.

This is an educational map of rules, execution,
risk,
and limits.
It is not a promise of profit.
We will separate a useful tool from a seductive
story.
The goal is not to find a magic bot.

The goal is to understand the complete decision
chain.
An order reaches an exchange.
Was it a person clicking a button?
Or a rule that a computer followed without emotion?

By financial year twenty twenty-four, twelve point
eight percent
of N S E cash-market gross turnover was classified
as algo.
That is not a claim about all Indian trading.
It is one scoped exchange measure.
In this video, we unpack what the machines actually
do.
A human can use the same rule manually.
Automation changes repeatability and speed.
It does not change what the rule knows, or
what the market can do next.
Part one. The anatomy.
An algorithm is not a magic prediction.
It is a repeatable chain of decisions.
Keep this map in mind through every strategy.
If one link is missing, the system is incomplete.
A signal alone is only an opinion.
A daily algo begins with data.
It turns data into a signal.

Then risk checks decide whether the signal deserves
an
order.
The broker routes the order.
The exchange matches it.
Fills return to the system.
So the loop is data, signal, risk, order, fill.

Every serious system also watches the loop, because
a
correct idea can still fail through bad data, a
rejected order, or a runaway process.
This chain also explains why daily algos are more
than a chart indicator.
A chart can suggest.
Risk decides.
Routing executes.
Monitoring checks that reality matches the plan.
Algo trading is a broad category.

High-frequency trading is a faster,
latency-sensitive subset.

Direct market access is an institutional route
through a
broker.

Co-location means systems are placed near exchange
infrastructure to
reduce delay.
These labels are not interchangeable.
On N S E cash market in financial year

twenty twenty-four, algo was twelve point eight
percent of
gross turnover.

Co-location was thirty-four point three percent, and
it is
not an algo share.
The I M F said algo was about seventy
percent of U S equities trading in October twenty
twenty-four.
That figure is U S only.
For a retail learner, the useful question is not
who is fastest.
It is what kind of system you are actually
describing.

Execution speed, access route, and trading logic are
separate
choices.
Most daily strategies are simple rule families.
Momentum follows a move.

Mean reversion bets a stretched move may return
toward
average.
Breakout trades a range boundary.
V W A P and T W A P
split a large order.
Market making quotes both sides.
Arbitrage compares related prices.
A rule is not an edge merely because it
has a name.

It needs suitable data, a tested condition, risk
limits,
and execution that survives its costs.
Think of these as different answers to one question.

Do you expect continuation, reversal, a range break,
cheaper

execution, liquidity provision, or a temporary price
mismatch?
Then define exactly when that answer is wrong.
Part two. The strategies.
These charts use illustrative synthetic data.
They are not backtests, history, or recommendations.
Synthetic examples let us see the rule clearly.
They do not show a return.

Real markets add noise, queues, spreads, gaps, and
competition.
Momentum asks whether a move is persistent.
One common rule compares a fast moving average with
a slow moving average.
When the fast line rises above the slow line,
the rule can permit a long position.
When it falls back below, the rule exits or
reverses.
The chart is illustrative synthetic data.
Its failure mode is chop.

In a sideways market, repeated crosses create
whipsaws.

The system pays spread, slippage, and charges while
repeatedly
being wrong.
The important discipline is consistency.

A trend follower cannot celebrate one winner and
skip
the next valid signal.
That would replace a rule with hindsight.
The rule needs a position size and a loss
limit too.
Mean reversion starts from a different belief.
A price far from its recent average may move
back toward it.

Bollinger bands frame a moving average with
volatility bands.
R S I is an oscillator from zero to
one hundred.
A low reading or lower-band poke can become an
entry condition.
The chart is illustrative synthetic data.
But a strong trend can keep going.
Cheap can become cheaper.
A band is a measurement, not a floor.
Mean reversion needs a definition of normal.
That definition is always historical and imperfect.
Before trading it, ask what news or regime could
make the old average irrelevant.
Pairs trading compares two related series.

The algo measures their spread, then a z-score
describes

how unusual that spread is against its recent
history.
A rule may act when the absolute z-score exceeds
two.
It goes long one leg and short the other,
expecting the relationship to normalize.
The chart is illustrative synthetic data.
The real danger is a broken relationship.

A sector shock, company event, or changing business
model
can make yesterday's pair irrelevant.
A pair is not safe merely because it has
moved together before.

The model needs synchronized data, a clear hedge
rule,
and a way to exit when the spread keeps
widening.
Neutral-looking positions still carry risk.

Opening-range breakout defines a first trading
window.
Its high and low become boundaries.
If price crosses above the high, a long rule
may activate.
If it crosses below the low, a short rule
may activate.
A stop defines failure before the order is sent.
The chart is illustrative synthetic data.

Opening noise, headline gaps, and false breakouts
are the
core danger.
A boundary crossed once is not a guaranteed trend.
A breakout rule must decide its range before the
break.
It must decide its stop before the entry.

Otherwise the system is just reacting after the
emotional
part of the move has arrived.
V W A P means volume-weighted average price.

It is an execution benchmark, not automatically a
directional
bet.
A large parent order can be divided into child
orders.
T W A P spaces those slices through time.
A V W A P schedule responds to traded
volume.
The goal is to reduce impact and compare fills
fairly.
The chart is illustrative synthetic data.

Poor volume forecasts, information leakage, missed
fills, and market
impact can still make execution expensive.
This distinction matters.
A V W A P algorithm can help execute
an investment decision.

It does not answer whether the investment decision
was
good.

Execution quality and market direction are different
problems.
Market makers quote a bid and an ask.
They can earn spread when both sides trade, while
controlling inventory.

Their danger is adverse selection: informed flow can
trade
against a stale quote.

Arbitrage instead compares related prices, such as
cash and
futures.
It buys one and sells the other only if
the spread survives every cost and constraint.

Legging, funding, limits, taxes, and execution can
erase an
apparent spread.
Small theoretical profits attract fast competition.
Both families sound mechanical because they are.
But neither removes market risk.
A spread is only useful after costs.
A quote is only useful while information has not
moved past it.
Part three. The India reality.
An API bot operates inside a broker and exchange
rulebook.
India-first means the operating details matter.
A rule that works in a notebook still has

to pass broker, identity, authentication, tagging,
and monitoring requirements.
S E B I issued the retail algo framework
on four February twenty twenty-five.
Under its glide path, the framework applies to all
stockbrokers from one April twenty twenty-six.
N S E's documented threshold is ten orders per
second per exchange and segment.
At or below that threshold, an API algo gets
a generic Algo I D.
Above it, the algo must register.

Access needs a unique key, broker-whitelisted static
I P,
OAuth, two-factor authentication, and daily logout.
Broker is principal. Provider is agent.
Audit trail is kept at least five years.

These are safeguards for traceability and
accountability.
They are not a scorecard for a strategy.

Registration or an identifier does not certify a
return.
It makes orders easier to identify and supervise.
Costs decide whether a fast strategy survives.

From one April twenty twenty-six, sell-side
securities futures S
T T is zero point zero five percent.
Option-sale S T T is zero point one five
percent of premium.

A Zerodha example lists futures brokerage at zero
point

zero three percent or twenty rupees per order,
whichever
is lower.
Options are twenty rupees per executed order.
That is one broker example, not all brokers.
N S E transaction charges and G S T
add more.

Spread, impact, delay, and missed fills are implicit
costs.
Gross return is not net return.
A robust test asks a tougher question.
What happens if fills are worse than expected?
What happens if the spread is wider?
What happens if a small gross edge disappears after
the complete cost stack?
Here is the uncomfortable scope-labelled evidence.
S E B I said ninety-three percent of over

one crore individual equity futures and options
traders lost

money between financial year twenty twenty-two and
twenty twenty-four.

Aggregate losses exceeded one point eight lakh crore
rupees.
Only one percent made more than one lakh rupees
after costs.

The financial year twenty twenty-four average
transaction cost was
twenty-six thousand rupees per individual trader.
This is an individual F and O study, not
an algo-user profitability study.
Automation does not create edge.
Backtest does not equal live trading.
Retail API does not equal H F T.
The lesson is not that every trader will lose.
The lesson is that broad retail F and O
outcomes are harsh, and a claim of automation does
not change that evidence.
Treat every profit promise with special caution.
Part four. Build and run one.
The code is only one component.
Controls make it a trading system.
Now we turn the map into an operating checklist.

The right order is deliberate: test first, limit
risk,
then observe what happens in the real environment.

The real stack starts with market data and
instrument
information.

Validate stale feeds, timestamps, missing values,
and market status.
Calculate the signal.
Convert it into a desired position.

Then risk checks cap cash, margin, exposure, order
size,
and daily loss.
An order-management system creates child orders.
The broker API routes tagged orders.
The exchange sends acknowledgements and fills.
Monitoring compares intent with reality.
A kill switch is part of the design, not
an emergency decoration.
Each hand-off should be observable.
You should be able to answer: what data arrived,

what signal fired, which check approved it, which
order
left, and which fill returned.
If you cannot answer that, you cannot safely debug
it.

A backtest replays historical data under
assumptions.

It should separate train, validation, and test
periods.
It must avoid look-ahead and survivorship bias.

It must model charges, spread, slippage, partial
fills, and
changing liquidity.
An overfit curve can look perfect in sample, then
flatten or fail in walk-forward trading.
The chart is illustrative synthetic data.

Live trading adds current queue position, outages,
rejected orders,

and market regimes that historical tests cannot
fully recreate.
A good backtest is a challenge to the idea,
not a sales brochure.
Change assumptions.
Reserve unseen data.
Stress costs.
If the result survives only one narrow setting, it
is fragile.

Pseudo-code should read like an accountable
decision.
First calculate a fast and slow average.
If the fast average is above the slow average,
propose a position.
Do not send it yet.
Check cash and margin.
Check maximum order size.
Check the daily loss limit.
Check the instrument is tradable and the data is
fresh.
Only then send the tagged order.
If any check fails, reject and alert.
The strongest line of code is often the one
that prevents a trade.
This is why risk code sits immediately before the
order.
The signal may be perfectly valid and still be

unacceptable today because cash, margin, size, or
loss limits
say no.
That is disciplined automation.
Going live begins smaller than a backtest fantasy.
Paper-trade first.
Use conservative position sizing.

Watch for stale data, rejected orders, duplicate
orders, latency

spikes, unexpected exposure, and daily-loss
breaches.

Reconcile exchange acknowledgements with the
intended position.
Alerts need an owner.
A kill switch needs a tested path.

Discipline matters more than clever code, because a
live
system trades the actual market, not a chart frozen
in hindsight.
Paper trading checks workflow.
Small live size checks execution.
Neither step proves future profitability.

They reduce the chance that a technical failure
becomes
a large financial mistake.
Keep five rules.
Model all explicit and implicit costs.
Test out of sample, not only where you tuned
the rule.
Size small enough that a normal loss is survivable.
Monitor every live component.

Treat promised, expected, or unverified past-return
marketing as a
red flag.
S E B I's restriction is nuanced: it does
not mean all performance discussion is banned.
It does mean brokers and platforms cannot make those

unverified return references, subject to the
specified verified-metrics route.
The common thread is humility.
Markets change.
Data fails.
Costs compound.

A system should be designed to survive uncertainty,
not
to advertise certainty.
So the whole map is this.
A trading algorithm is a rule connected to data,
risk, routing, and monitoring.

Strategies differ, but all can fail through costs,
bad
assumptions, or a changing market.

India adds broker, API, identity, tagging, and audit
controls.
Automation is not edge.

Educational information from public sources, not
investment advice. Consult
a S E B I-registered adviser.
Thanks for watching.
Keep the scope labels attached to every number.
Keep synthetic examples labelled.
And keep the decision to stop as available as
the decision to trade.
